source.basis: Operator facility page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
DartPoints Cincinnati publishes 1.6 MW of IT capacity. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, that is roughly 40 racks; at 10 kW per rack, a more typical colocation density, it is roughly 160 racks. Either way, the footprint is small by the standards of AI infrastructure, where a single large training cluster can consume tens of megawatts. Certifications and redundancy tier are not published on the operator's spec page.

Ohio has 76 mapped facilities, of which only 5 publish a megawatt figure, totaling 38.6 MW across those five. DartPoints Cincinnati ranks fifth among that group, meaning it is the smallest of the five facilities for which a number exists. It represents 1.6 of 38.6 published megawatts, or about 4 percent of the state's published IT capacity, though that denominator covers only a fraction of the state's actual installed base.

For a reader deciding whether this campus matters to AI, the honest answer the data supports is: probably not at scale. At 1.6 MW, the facility is sized for enterprise colocation or edge workloads, not for the multi-megawatt GPU clusters that define frontier training or large inference deployments. It could host a small inference endpoint or a regional edge node, but nothing in the published numbers suggests it is positioned as a primary AI compute site. Expansion plans, power availability from the local grid, and any AI-specific cooling or networking infrastructure are not published.
